newsitem.title: USA: Judge allows Washington tobacco case to proceed.
newsitem.headline: Judge allows Washington tobacco case to proceed.

text.p: A judge in Washington Tuesday cleared the way for the state to proceed with its lawsuit against the tobacco industry.

In a 15-page ruling, King County Superior Court Judge George Finkle dismissed two of the state's claims but let its other claims stand, allowing officials to pursue antitrust and consumer protection aspects of its case.

"The heart of our case -- to protect children and hold the tobacco industry accountable for decades of public deception about their product -- will now go forward," State Attorney General Chris Gregoire said in a statement. "Judge Finkle has given us the green light to proceed with an action that will change the unacceptable conduct of this multi-billion dollar industry."

In June, the state Attorney General's office filed a lawsuit against some of the nation's biggest tobacco firms alleging they violated state consumer protection and antitrust laws by illegally targeting minors, suppressing information about addiction and the health consequences of smoking, deceptively increasing the addictive potency of the nicotine in their product, and conspiring to prevent the development of safer tobacco products.
In September the tobacco companies filed a motion seeking to have the majority of the state's claims dismissed.
Among the claims Finkle dismissed was one that would have forced the industry to pay the state for some of Medicaid expenses paid to residents who had illnesses allegedly caused by smoking.
RJ Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp's RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co, hailed the decision Tuesday.

"Judge Finkle's reasoning of the law in this opinion is consistent with our long-held contention that to bring a Medicaid recoupment claim, the state must stand in the shoes' of those it purports to represent," Daniel Donahue, senior vice president for the company, said in statement.
The judge scheduled oral arguments for six discovery motions for Jan. 9.
